 'Independent counts': Matthew McConaughey's wild 6-minute political rant receives mixed reactions from fans
 Matthew McConaughey took to X to encourage independents to realise their voting power ahead of early voting in the US midterm elections, but his call to break away from the two-party system has been called "tone deaf" and "irresponsible" by Republicans and Democrats on social media.
 Jaimee Marshall Lifestyle Reporter 3 min read October 19, 2026 - 1:58PM Matthew McConaughey has turned his attention to the upcoming US midterm elections in a six-minute video posted to social media.
 The 56-year-old actor encouraged Americans to break away from the two-party system by seriously considering the role independents play in keeping both parties in check and dispelling notions people have about independents being "fence-sitters" who don't know what they believe.
 “They’ve been telling us for years that an independent vote is a wasted vote,” McConaughey opened the clip, before asking viewers how that "unwasted vote" has been working out for them.
 The True Detective star clarified he was not there to endorse any candidate or party but rather to educate people about the upcoming ballot and endorse only two things: fairness and reality.
 Matthew McConaughey arrives at the Los Angeles premiere of Apple TV's "Brothers" at Hammer Museum on September 17, 2026. Picture: Maya Dehlin/WireImage Matthew McConaughey on the sideline during the Allstate Red River Rivalry between the Texas Longhorns and Oklahoma Sooners on October 10, 2026, at Cotton Bowl Stadium in Dallas. Picture: David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images McConaughey argued that the current system gives Democrats and Republicans far too much influence and called for a "fair fight" where "fighters who ought to be represented in the fight are actually in the fight."
 "The number one political identity in America today is not Republican. It is not Democrat. It is independent," McConaughey claimed, adding that there are "more of us than either party."
 He added that if the majority of Americans identify as independents, they belong on the ballot as a real potential winner to be considered by voters, not as a "protest".
 Independent counts. pic.twitter.com/N9MkKlBuIR 
— Matthew McConaughey (@McConaughey) October 18, 2026 
 McConaughey then launched into his signature poetic storytelling style.
 "Before there was ever Republican or Democrat, there was an American. Our birth certificate is not the Declaration of Compromise. It is the Declaration of Independence."
 McConaughey argued that a "true independent" isn't a fence-sitter or someone who doesn't know how they feel, nor is it someone who is even against the Republicans and Democrats. 
 "A true independent takes the best of both," McConaughey said, adding: "That's not indecision; it's judgment."
 A few minutes in, the actor revealed the reason for the tangent, citing a system that has never been more lopsided.
 McConaughey argued that 87 per cent of the US house seats in 2024 were effectively decided in party primaries by just 7 per cent of eligible voters and that, for most Americans, the election is over before they even show up in November. 
 Steelmanning the argument that most independents vote partisan anyway, McConaughey granted that's true, but added that's only because, in most races, the parties are the only real choice on the ballot.
 "The truth of it is, we don’t know how many independents would vote for a true independent – organised, funded, owned by neither side – because no one has ever given us one."
 The native Texan argued that independents are the perfect mechanism for bringing the parties back to the middle, where "most American values live".
 Using a football analogy, McConaughey says if the two parties want to play the whole game in their own end zones, independents keep the game between the 40s.
 The Oscar winner threw in his tacit support for the ethos behind the Independent Leadership Council, which was launched by former Senator Joe Manchin and his daughter.
 It's a nonprofit organisation that has vowed to recruit, fund, and back true independent candidates for Congress.
 McConaughey clarified he wasn't endorsing the organisation, merely supporting the idea of empowering Americans to have more fair elections with more options.
 The actor and writer added that the midterm elections are coming up this November, with early voting already underway, and there will reportedly be more than two choices on the ballot in more places than ever. 
 While it is not known whether McConaughey anticipated such swift backlash from both major parties, that's certainly what he got.
 Many accused the actor of reading off "AI slop", pointing to the excessive use of negative parallelism like, "It's not X, it's Y."
 Others even shared screenshots from Pangram, an AI detector that was showing "100 per cent AI-generated" results.
 On X, his video was flooded with comments accusing him of encouraging people to throw away their vote, which would "guarantee Democrat communists win," and told him to "stick to movies".
 Many ripped the Texan as a "fence-sitter" for refusing to endorse a candidate in the contentious Texas Senate race, where Democrat James Talarico is running against Republican Ken Paxton.
 One X user said, “Matthew McConaughey, who in 2021 the Texas Tribune reported had voted just twice in the past decade, lectures us on elections before early voting starts tomorrow.”
 Former The Hills reality star turned politician Spencer Pratt argued that this isn't a "Republicans vs Dems" issue, but a "people who hate America vs people who love it" issue, and claimed a third party wouldn't fix that.
 On Instagram, the actor caught heat from the opposite end of the political spectrum, who called the actor's bid for less partisan extremism "irresponsible."
 “I’m exhausted by this rhetoric when we are in a fully fascist state," one person commented.

 More “No Kings” demonstrations have erupted around the nation to encourage Americans to vote early in the midterm elections, which will determine which party will control congress.
 Republicans currently hold a slim majority in the House and a clear majority in the Senate.
